name: borsh (Binary Object Representation Serializer for Hashing)
verdict_reason: borsh.io says skipping serde makes borsh faster than bincode in some cases. In the independent 2026-08-07 run borsh 1.8.0 was within 11% of bincode 1.3.3 everywhere: slower on log and mesh, and 4%-7% faster only on minecraft_savedata. That is not a measurable speed advantage; borsh's real selling point is a canonical, hash-stable encoding.
tier_reason: Third-party benchmark with public code; rustc nightly, the CPU and lto = true are stated.
claimed_speedup: Serialize 481.77 µs vs 464.75 µs (log, slower), 5.3728 ms vs 4.8569 ms (mesh, slower), 485.09 µs vs 518.86 µs (minecraft_savedata, 1.07x faster); deserialize 1.6997 ms vs 1.6158 ms (slower), 3.7284 ms vs 3.6395 ms (slower), 1.4610 ms vs 1.5229 ms (1.04x faster) (ratios derived from page data)
workload: rust_serialization_benchmark log, mesh and minecraft_savedata datasets with borsh's own derives.
toolchain: rustc 1.99.0-nightly (2026-08-06), bench profile lto = true, no target-cpu flag
one_liner: Canonical binary format from NEAR for hashing and consensus; benchmarks at the same speed as bincode 1.3, not faster.
how_it_is_fast: Uses its own BorshSerialize/BorshDeserialize derives instead of serde and a simple fixed layout (little-endian integers, length-prefixed collections). The benchmark shows this lands at about bincode's speed.
use_it_when: You need a bijective encoding whose bytes are stable for hashing or signing
Interop with NEAR or Solana programs that already speak borsh
skip_it_when: Speed is the reason for switching from bincode: wincode, bitcode or rkyv are several times faster in the same run
caveats: borsh.io's own benchmarks are charts from a Google Cloud n1-standard-2 run with no text numbers
tradeoffs: RUSTSEC-2023-0033 (unsound parsing of non-Copy zero-sized types) affected versions before 1.0.0-alpha.1 and 0.10.4
